procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Judicial Magistrate 1st Class, Margao
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated June 19, 1969 of the Judicial Commissioner's Court, Goa, Daman and Diu in Criminal Revision Application 23 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State filed a revision application under s. 435 of the Indian Code of Criminal Procedure to the Judicial Commissioner's Court, Goa, Daman & Diu. The Judicial Commissioner allowed the revision, concluding that the order of November 6, 1963, was ultra vires.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the judgment and order of the Judicial Commissioner.

decision.appeal_result:
In the result the appeal is allowed, the judgment and order 
of. the Judicial Commissioner set aside and that of the learned 
Sessions Judge restored.

issue.issue_text: Whether the order passed by the Lt. Governor on November 6, 1963, was invalid.

facts: The Lt. Governor of Goa, Daman & Diu passed an order on November 6, 1963, to address difficulties regarding criminal procedure for offences committed before new laws came into force.
The order itself stated that it was made under the authority of the 'Goa, Daman and Diu (Administration) Removal of Difficulties Order, 1962'.
law: The Court acknowledged that the cited authority, the 'Removal of Difficulties Order, 1962', did not actually grant the Lt. Governor the power to pass the order in question.

However, the Court identified another law, Section 8 of the Goa, Daman and Diu (Laws) Regulation, 1962, which did authorize the Lt. Governor to make provisions for the removal of difficulties in applying newly extended laws.

The Court applied the legal principle that if a government authority has the legal power to perform an act, the act is valid even if the authority mistakenly cites the wrong law or source of power in its order.
application: The Court found that the Lt. Governor was competent to make provisions to remove the difficulties that had arisen in applying the new criminal procedure laws.

Although the order incorrectly cited the 'Removal of Difficulties Order, 1962' as its source of power, the Court determined that the order could be legally justified under the authority granted by Section 8 of the 1962 Regulation.
The existence of a valid source of power (Section 8) was sufficient to uphold the order, regardless of the error in citation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the order was invalid. It held that because the Lt. Governor had the substantive power to issue the order under Section 8 of the 1962 Regulation, the order was valid despite its reference to an incorrect legal provision.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 8 of the Regulation, which authorized the Lt. Governor to make provisions for the removal of difficulties, justified the passing of the impugned order.

facts: The Lt. Governor of Goa, Daman and Diu passed an order concerning the procedure for criminal proceedings.
The order mistakenly cited the 'Goa, Daman and Diu (Administration) Removal of Difficulties Order, 1962' as its source of power, which both parties agreed did not authorize the order.
The appellant (the state) argued that the order was nevertheless valid because it could be justified under a different law, namely Section 8 of the Goa, Daman and Diu (Laws) Regulation, 1962.
The court noted that "some difficulties were experienced" regarding the application of the new criminal procedure law, which prompted the Lt. Governor to pass the order.
law: Section 8 of the Regulation empowers the Central Government to make provisions to remove any "difficulty" that arises in giving effect to laws extended to the territory.
Under the General Clauses Act, the Lt. Governor, as the Administrator of Goa, Daman and Diu, is entitled to exercise the powers of the Central Government.

Citing the majority opinion in *Jalan Trading Co. v. Mill Mazdoor Union*, the court held that the word "difficulty" should not be construed narrowly (i.e., limited to a specific concrete case), but broadly, authorizing the government to determine for itself what constitutes a difficulty and how to remove it.
application: The Court first established that an order is not invalid simply because it cites the wrong source of power, as long as a valid source of power exists.
It determined that the Lt. Governor was legally empowered to act under Section 8, as his role as Administrator allowed him to exercise the powers of the Central Government.

Applying the broad interpretation of "difficulty" from the *Jalan Trading* case, the Court found that the Lt. Governor was competent to identify the procedural issues as "difficulties" and to pass the impugned order to remove them.
Therefore, the Court concluded that Section 8 of the Regulation provided the necessary legal authority for the Lt. Governor's order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument, concluding that Section 8 of the Regulation clearly authorized the Lt. Governor to pass the impugned order. The Court held that the order was valid because the Lt. Governor had the authority of the Central Government and the term "difficulty" in Section 8 was to be interpreted broadly, giving him the power to resolve the issues he had identified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the order passed by the Lt. Governor on November 6, 1963, was invalid.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the order was valid, relying on the power granted to the Lt. Governor under the law (specifically Section 8 of the Regulation).
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the State) argued that the order was invalid, a position that had been upheld by the Judicial Commissioner.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 8 of the Regulation, which authorized the Lt. Governor to make provisions for the removal of difficulties, justified the passing of the impugned order.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that Section 8 of the Regulation did justify the order. They countered the respondent's argument by pointing out that the legal precedent cited by the respondent was a minority opinion, and the majority opinion in that case supported a broader interpretation of the word 'difficulty' which would authorize the Lt. Governor's order.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that Section 8 did not justify the order. They contended that the term 'difficulty' in Section 8 should be interpreted very narrowly, citing observations from a judge in a previous case. They also argued that the order was not justified because there was no 'concrete case' of difficulty when the order was made.

cases.case_name: Jalan Trading Co. (Private) Ltd. v. Mill Mazdoor Union
cases.principle: For the interpretation of the word 'difficulty' in a 'removal of difficulties' clause. The Court relied on the majority opinion (by Shah, J.) which did not give a limited meaning to the word and held that such a section authorized the Government to determine the purposes of the Act and make provisions for the removal of doubts or difficulties.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order issued by a government authority is not invalid for citing an incorrect source of power, so long as a valid source of power for the order exists. A statutory provision empowering the government to make provisions for the "removal of difficulty" grants that government the authority to determine for itself what constitutes a difficulty and to issue orders to resolve it.
obiter: Neither the appellant nor the respondent has urged before us that s. 8 of the Regulation itself is invalid.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the impugned order passed by the Lt. Governor was valid because Section 8 of the Regulation provided the necessary legal authority. The court reasoned that an order is not invalid merely because it cites the wrong source of power, so long as a legitimate source of power exists. In interpreting Section 8, the court rejected the respondent's argument for a narrow definition of 'difficulty,' which was based on a minority judicial opinion in a prior case. Instead, the court adopted the broader interpretation from the majority opinion in the same precedent, which held that the government was authorized to determine for itself the difficulties that required removal.
legal_tests_applied: An official action is valid if a source of power for that action subsists under any law, even if the authority invokes an incorrect law or order when taking the action.
